candidates.quote: In spring it is the dawn that is most beautiful.
candidates.author: Sei Shōnagon
candidates.locator: section 1, the opening sentence (The Pillow Book of Sei Shōnagon, Columbia University Press, 1967, vol. 1, p. 1)
candidates.whyThisMonth: The oldest first sentence in the slate is about the dawn itself, so a reader at six in the morning is standing exactly where the book begins.

candidates.quote: Everything in the world began with a yes.
candidates.author: Clarice Lispector
candidates.locator: the opening sentence of the narrative, after the dedication (Carcanet, 1986)
candidates.whyThisMonth: A first sentence that says beginning is an act of assent, which is what a new year asks of the reader before anything is proved.
candidates.speaker: Rodrigo S.M., the narrator

candidates.quote: Barrabás came to us by sea, the child Clara wrote in her delicate calligraphy.
candidates.author: Isabel Allende
candidates.locator: chapter 1, Rosa the Beautiful, the opening sentence (Knopf, 1985)
candidates.whyThisMonth: The novel opens with a child writing its first line and closes by writing it again, so the book is itself a lesson in beginning twice.

candidates.quote: I hope I will be able to confide everything to you, as I have never been able to confide in anyone, and I hope you will be a great source of comfort and support.
candidates.author: Anne Frank
candidates.work: The Diary of a Young Girl: The Definitive Edition
candidates.locator: entry of 12 June 1942, the first entry (Doubleday, 1995)
candidates.whyThisMonth: The first line of the most read diary in the world is a thirteen-year-old opening a blank book on her birthday and making it a promise, which is what a January page is.

candidates.quote: Every limit is a beginning as well as an ending.
candidates.author: George Eliot
candidates.whyThisMonth: The last section of the great English novel opens by saying that an ending is a beginning, which is the whole argument of the first of January in nine words.

candidates.quote: Mrs. Dalloway said she would buy the flowers herself.
candidates.author: Virginia Woolf
candidates.whyThisMonth: A whole day, and a whole novel, begins with one small decision to do a thing yourself, which is the size of resolve a morning can actually carry.

candidates.quote: Ships at a distance have every man’s wish on board.
candidates.author: Zora Neale Hurston
candidates.locator: chapter 1, the opening sentence (J. B. Lippincott, 1937)
candidates.whyThisMonth: The first sentence puts every wish the reader has out on the horizon, still sailing, which is the honest condition of a year that has not started yet.

candidates.quote: Marilla, isn’t it nice to think that tomorrow is a new day with no mistakes in it yet?
candidates.author: L. M. Montgomery
candidates.locator: chapter 21, A New Departure in Flavorings, the closing exchange (L. C. Page, 1908)
candidates.whyThisMonth: Said after a cake ruined with liniment, it is the plainest statement in fiction of what a fresh day is for, and it comes with Marilla’s dry reply built in.
candidates.speaker: Anne Shirley

candidates.quote: Risk! Risk anything! Care no more for the opinion of others, for those voices. Do the hardest thing on earth for you. Act for yourself. Face the truth.
candidates.author: Katherine Mansfield
candidates.locator: entry of 14 October 1922, her last birthday, ed. J. Middleton Murry (Constable, 1927)
candidates.whyThisMonth: Written to herself on a birthday three months before she died, it is a beginning-again resolution in five short commands, and the reader can take them one at a time.

candidates.quote: We tell ourselves stories in order to live.
candidates.author: Joan Didion
candidates.locator: the title essay, the opening sentence (Simon and Schuster, 1979)
candidates.whyThisMonth: The most quoted first sentence in American essay writing says the story we tell about the year ahead is not decoration but survival, so the January page is doing real work.

candidates.quote: This book was written in good faith, reader.
candidates.author: Michel de Montaigne
candidates.locator: To the Reader, the opening sentence (The Complete Essays of Montaigne, Stanford University Press, 1957, p. 2)
candidates.whyThisMonth: The first sentence of the book that invented the essay is a promise made before a single page is proved, which is the exact shape of a resolution.

candidates.quote: But that is the beginning of a new story—the story of the gradual renewal of a man, the story of his gradual regeneration, of his passing from one world into another, of his initiation into a new unknown life.
candidates.author: Fyodor Dostoevsky
candidates.whyThisMonth: The novel ends by refusing to end, calling renewal a story that has only just started, which tells a reader on the first of the month that the hard part is allowed to be gradual.

candidates.quote: And it seemed as though in a little while the solution would be found, and then a new and splendid life would begin; and it was clear to both of them that they had still a long, long road before them, and that the most complicated and difficult part of it was only just beginning.
candidates.author: Anton Chekhov
candidates.locator: section IV, the closing sentence (The Lady with the Dog and Other Stories, Chatto and Windus, 1917)
candidates.whyThisMonth: The most famous unresolved ending in the short story says a new life is beginning and that the difficult part is ahead, which is honest company for anyone starting over.

candidates.quote: A book must be the axe for the frozen sea inside us.
candidates.author: Franz Kafka
candidates.work: Letters to Friends, Family, and Editors
candidates.locator: letter to Oskar Pollak, 27 January 1904 (Schocken, 1977, p. 16)
candidates.whyThisMonth: A January letter from a twenty-year-old about what reading is for, and the frozen sea is the reader’s own at the start of the year.

candidates.quote: You are about to begin reading Italo Calvino’s new novel, If on a winter’s night a traveler.
candidates.author: Italo Calvino
candidates.work: If on a winter’s night a traveler
candidates.locator: chapter 1, the opening sentence (Harcourt Brace Jovanovich, 1981, p. 3)
candidates.whyThisMonth: The only famous first sentence that is entirely about the act of beginning, addressed to you, on a winter’s night, which is the month to the letter.

candidates.quote: For actually the earth had no roads to begin with, but when many men pass one way, a road is made.
candidates.author: Lu Xun
candidates.locator: the closing sentence (Selected Stories of Lu Hsun, Foreign Languages Press, Peking, 1960)
candidates.whyThisMonth: The story ends with hope defined as a road that exists only because people started walking, so the first step of the year is the whole argument.
candidates.speaker: the narrator
